label: Hydrogen sulphide (sour gas)
summary: Hydrogen sulphide (H2S) is a colourless, flammable gas found in sour oil and gas in Alberta, Saskatchewan and northeast BC, and in sewage and manure. It smells of rotten eggs at low levels, but from about 100 ppm it dulls and then numbs your sense of smell, from about 500 ppm it can drop you within minutes, and at around 1,000 ppm a breath or two is enough. It is heavier than air and collects in low ground and tanks.
signs: Oil and gas wells, oil tanks and pipelines; in Saskatchewan, sour gas comes up with the oil at many wells
Fixed gas monitors with alarms, and 'Danger, Deadly Gases' signs at manure pits and pump-out points
A rotten-egg smell, which turns sickly sweet at higher levels. A smell that fades while you're still there is a danger sign, not good news
Stinging, watering eyes, sore throat, cough, headache, nausea or dizziness near a site
Low spots: ditches, hollows, basements, pits, sewers and the insides of tanks, especially downwind of a site
Oil tank hatches: lone workers who opened them to gauge tanks have been found collapsed from oxygen-poor air and hydrocarbon vapour, even with no H2S
Sewers, septic tanks, manure pits and lift stations make H2S too (see Confined spaces: pits, tanks, wells, silos)
do: Approach oil and gas sites from upwind and uphill
If you smell rotten eggs or your eyes start to sting, leave at once, upwind and uphill, and don't go back to check
Keep at least 100 m (330 ft) from a leak in every direction, and stay upwind and uphill
Trust a gas alarm over your nose
Work in pairs, in sight of each other, around tanks and wells
dont: Don't open tank hatches, valves or pipes at oil and gas sites, or climb tanks to look in
Don't trust your nose: at high levels you smell nothing, so no smell never means safe air
Don't go into low ground, pits or buildings on a site, or downwind hollows, while there's any sign of a leak
Don't go into gas after someone who has collapsed without breathing apparatus, and never into a pit, tank, sewer or hollow: rescuers collapse too (see Confined spaces: pits, tanks, wells, silos)
Don't make sparks or flames near a leak: H2S explodes at 4.3 to 45% in air, and burning it makes sulphur dioxide, which also stings eyes and lungs
ppe: Dust masks do nothing against H2S, and even masks with H2S-rated cartridges or canisters are rated only to 100 ppm. Alberta's farm guide and the emergency guidebook call for air-supplied breathing apparatus (SCBA)

A personal H2S monitor with an alarm, bump-tested before each day's use. It sees only H2S: at oil tanks and hatches, where low oxygen and hydrocarbon vapour have killed with no H2S, wear a multi-gas monitor that also reads oxygen and flammable gas
firstAid: Rescue only in breathing apparatus, or from clear air upwind and out of low ground. Never go into a pit, tank, sewer or hollow after them: a breath or two can drop you too (see Confined spaces: pits, tanks, wells, silos)
Move them to fresh air upwind; if they aren't breathing normally, start CPR, with a mouth shield if you have one: gas can come off their clothing, skin and breath
Rinse stinging eyes with gently running water for at least 20 minutes
Anyone knocked down, or with a cough or chest pain afterwards, can develop chemical pneumonia: keep them resting and watched; they need medical care
